title: Seònaid Mhòr cuts paired marks at Ros dhomhain
summary: The keeper of the Ros dhomhain tide-rock takes to cutting two strokes for every tide instead of one, a mark for the water's highest reach and a shorter mark beside it for its lowest ebb, so that whoever reads the rock after her has the whole of the water's motion and not only its rising.

title: The spacing of the marks travels without its reasoning
summary: Households at Inis thais's own harbour, hearing only that Ros dhomhain's keeper cuts her marks at a certain interval, begin cutting their own high-water marks at that same spacing on a rock of their own, though none of them can say why that width and no other.

title: Peigi Dhubh calls for a landing of laid stone
summary: At the household's board, Lachlann Ruadh's daughter says plainly that a hill whose wealth now travels by water deserves better than an open shingle beach a winter tide can rearrange. Her father agrees, and the households of the Red Hill give a season's labour to the work.

title: The stone landing is set at the river-mouth
summary: Course on course of quarried stone is laid where the fresh water of the lake meets the tide from the sea, until a boat can come alongside at any state of the water without a hand needed to haul it clear of the mud: the Red Hill's first way onto open water that does not depend on a beach's mercy.

title: Houses draw in round the rock and the landing
summary: Boats from harbours further down the coast begin putting in at the new landing rather than carrying on to open beaches, and the scattered houses of that shore draw in closer round the tide-rock and the stone together until some sixty stand there, their people fishing now from boats of their own building.

title: Lachlann Ruadh falls ill
summary: A chill taken wading the shallows to right a boat settles in Lachlann an Altraim's chest and will not lift with the spring. He is five-and-sixty years old, an age the Red Hill reckons past complaint for a man who has spent his whole life wet to the knee in cold water.

title: Lachlann asks that the fostering be ended
summary: On one of his last evenings Lachlann tells his daughter that a fostering kept a season too long stops being a kindness and becomes only a habit no one has ended, and asks her not to let her own fondness be the reason the peace of the ford goes one day longer without its proper marking.

title: Lachlann Ruadh dies at five-and-sixty
summary: He dies in the hall he was born in, his daughter's hand in his own, the household gathered at the door with no closer claim on the bedside than the years they gave the hill. He held the Red Hill one-and-sixty years.

title: Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill at forty
summary: She sits down at the board the morning after her father's burial and asks for the tallies before she asks for anything else. The Red Hill's own steward says afterward that she keeps them straighter than her father ever did.

title: Peigi tells the fosterling he is to go home
summary: Walking the new stone landing with him in the last light of an evening, Peigi says her father was right, and that she means to send him home before the year turns, with salt enough for a household to carry as gift and not as trade, so the hill of Dùn ìseal will know he is sent back with honour.

title: Seònaid Mhòr cuts a last pair of marks for him
summary: On the evening before the train leaves, the keeper of the tide-rock cuts one more pair of marks at the rock's edge, though the tide calls for none, and will not say plainly what they are for beyond that the rock has marked every tide of his years there and should mark the last of them too.

title: The foster-son of Dùn ìseal comes home
summary: He walks the salt road east with a train of laden pack-beasts and three of the Red Hill's household, and comes in sight of the hill of the Stone Kings on the seventh evening, four-and-twenty years after he first walked the same road west at six years old.

title: Calum Ciar does not know his own brother
summary: Meeting the Red Hill's train at the gate in his mother's stead, Calum Ciar asks the fosterling which of the household he might be, a lake wind and four-and-twenty years having left nothing in him his brother's eye could fasten on as kin.

title: Eilidh Ghlas knows her son at the door
summary: Carried out to the hall door, Eilidh speaks her younger son's name before he has said a word to tell her who he is, and weeps and holds him a long while before she lets even her elder son greet him in turn.

title: The salt refrain is sung at the pans of Baile ghorm
summary: At the fires of the salt-rakers he teaches, without meaning to teach anything, the four-line refrain sung at the crust on the Red Hill's own lake shore. An old raker keeps it whole from a single hearing, and it runs on afterward at the sea-shore pans in words the Red Hill itself can no longer wholly construe.

title: The Stone Kings' list keeps him no name
summary: When the reciters after Eilidh set down her reign and her sons, Calum Ciar takes his place among the holders as every holder before him; of the one who went to the Red Hill and came home grown, no year, no reign and no deed is written, and the list stands as if she bore only the one son.
